mainEntity.name: How do you calculate the unit price?

acceptedAnswer.text: Divide the pack price by the number of units in the pack. A $24.00 case of 12 works out at $2.00 a unit.

mainEntity.name: How do you calculate cost per pound?

acceptedAnswer.text: Multiply the units by the net weight of each, then divide the pack price by that total. $24.00 over 12 units of 2 lb is 24 lb, so $1.00 a pound.

mainEntity.name: Which one should you compare on?

acceptedAnswer.text: Per pound, whenever the two packs hold different unit sizes. Per unit is only a fair comparison when a unit of one is the same thing as a unit of the other.

mainEntity.name: Can the cheaper pack per unit be the more expensive buy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, and it is the usual case. Option B is $1.67 a unit against A's $2.00, but B's units are lighter, so per pound B costs $1.11 and A costs $1.00.

mainEntity.name: What if you do not know the net weight?

acceptedAnswer.text: The calculator falls back to a per-unit comparison. Treat that as a rough answer and get the weight off the spec sheet before you move an account onto the pack.

mainEntity.name: Should landed cost go in instead of the supplier price?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, if you have it. Freight and handling attach to the pack, so a bulky case can lose a comparison it won on the supplier invoice.

mainEntity.name: How do you spot a supplier shrinking a pack?

acceptedAnswer.text: Watch cost per pound, not pack price. A unit going from 2 lb to 1.5 lb at the same price is a price rise that never shows on the invoice.
